Description
I could be making some sort of very simple mistake here. I've used jax2tf several times in the past and it has worked fine, but I've just tried to use it today and it's producing weird graphs. I chiselled my code down to a minimal example, and it was still happening, so I copy-pasted the readme code and it's happening with that too:
def sincos(x):
  return jnp.sin(jnp.cos(x))

my_model = tf.Module()
my_model.f = tf.function(jax2tf.convert(sincos), autograph=False, jit_compile=True, input_signature=[tf.TensorSpec([], tf.float32)])
tf.saved_model.save(my_model, './sincos', options=tf.saved_model.SaveOptions(experimental_custom_gradients=True))
I also tried this:
def multiply(a, b):
  return a * b

my_model = tf.Module()
my_model.f = tf.function(jax2tf.convert(multiply, with_gradient=False), autograph=False, jit_compile=True, input_signature=[
    tf.TensorSpec([3, 3], tf.float32, name="a"),
    tf.TensorSpec([3, 3], tf.float32, name="b"),
])
tf.saved_model.save(my_model, './multiply')
Here's a Colab notebook so you can quickly reproduce (Runtime > Run all):
https://colab.research.google.com/gist/josephrocca/5c847d793eed1efb67a6566b616eb467/simple-jax2tf-hello-world-example.ipynb
Here's a netron.app screenshot of the multiply model's graph:

nodes.bodyText:
Description
Here's a collab to reproduce the issue. I'll repeat it here with annotation.
I'd like to write a custom_vjp for a function involving a BCOO sparse matrix. I've minified my example to consider the toy case of matrix-vector multiplication.
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.experimental.sparse import BCOO 
from jax import grad, jit, vmap
from jax import custom_jvp, custom_vjp

# variable parameter
p = jnp.array(1.0)
# constants
b = jnp.array([2.0,3.0])
x = jnp.array([-3.0,2.0])

#############################################################
# Dense version without custom function
#############################################################

# E(p) = ‖ A(p) b - x ‖²
def E_dense(p):
    a = jnp.array([jnp.cos(p),-jnp.sin(p),jnp.sin(p),jnp.cos(p)])
    # build a dense matrix that depense on p
    I = jnp.array([0,1,0,1])
    J = jnp.array([0,0,1,1])
    A = jnp.zeros((2,2)).at[(I,J)].set(a)
    return jnp.linalg.norm(A@b - x)**2

print("E_dense(p): %g" % E_dense(p))
print("∇E_dense(p): %g" % grad(E_dense)(p))
print("----------------------------------------------------")

#############################################################
# Sparse version without custom_vjp
#############################################################

def E_sparse(p):
    a = jnp.array([jnp.cos(p),-jnp.sin(p),jnp.sin(p),jnp.cos(p)])
    I = jnp.array([0,1,0,1])
    J = jnp.array([0,0,1,1])
    A = BCOO((a,jnp.vstack((I,J)).T), shape=(2,2))
    return jnp.linalg.norm(A@b - x)**2

print("E_sparse(p): %g" % E_sparse(p))
print("∇E_sparse(p): %g" % grad(E_sparse)(p))
print("----------------------------------------------------")


#############################################################
# Dense version using custom_vjp
#############################################################

@custom_vjp
def mm_dense(A,b):
    return A @ b

def mm_dense_fwd(A,b):
    return mm_dense(A,b), (A,b)

def mm_dense_bwd(res,g):
    A,b = res
    partial1 = (jnp.outer(g , b))
    partial2 = (A.T  @ g)
    print("[mm_dense_bwd] partial1:")
    print(partial1)
    return ( partial1 , partial2 )

mm_dense.defvjp(mm_dense_fwd, mm_dense_bwd)

def E_dense_mm(p):
    a = jnp.array([jnp.cos(p),-jnp.sin(p),jnp.sin(p),jnp.cos(p)])
    I = jnp.array([0,1,0,1])
    J = jnp.array([0,0,1,1])
    A = jnp.zeros((2,2)).at[(I,J)].set(a,unique_indices=True)
    return jnp.linalg.norm(mm_dense(A,b) - x)**2

print("E_dense_mm(p): %g" % E_dense_mm(p))
print("∇E_dense_mm(p): %g" % grad(E_dense_mm)(p))
print("----------------------------------------------------")

#############################################################
# Sparse version using custom_vjp
#############################################################

# Given a vector, construct a sparse diagonal matrix
def diag_BCOO(b):
    indices = jnp.vstack((jnp.arange(0,len(b)),jnp.arange(0,len(b)))).T
    return BCOO( (b, indices), shape=(len(b),len(b)))

@custom_vjp
def mm_sparse(A,b):
    return A @ b

def mm_sparse_fwd(A,b):
    # cache the sparsity pattern of A
    S = BCOO((jnp.ones_like(A.data),A.indices),shape=A.shape)
    return mm_sparse(A,b), (A,b,S)

def mm_sparse_bwd(res,g):
    A,b,S = res
    partial1 = diag_BCOO(g) @ S @ diag_BCOO(b)
    # 🥝 This works even though it's returning the wrongly transposed partial
    #partial1 = diag_BCOO(b) @ S.T @ diag_BCOO(g)
    # 🍌 This also works, so it seems the final .T doesn't change anything
    #partial1 = (diag_BCOO(b) @ S.T @ diag_BCOO(g)).T
    print("[mm_sparse_bwd] partial1:")
    print(partial1.todense())
    partial2 = (A.T  @ g)
    return (partial1 , partial2)

mm_sparse.defvjp(mm_sparse_fwd, mm_sparse_bwd)

# E(p) = ‖ A(p) b - x ‖²
def E_sparse_mm(p):
    a = jnp.array([jnp.cos(p),-jnp.sin(p),jnp.sin(p),jnp.cos(p)])
    I = jnp.array([0,1,0,1])
    J = jnp.array([0,0,1,1])
    A = BCOO((a,jnp.vstack((I,J)).T), shape=(2,2))
    return jnp.linalg.norm(mm_sparse(A,b) - x)**2

print("E_sparse_mm(p): %g" % E_sparse_mm(p))
print("∇E_sparse_mm(p): %g" % grad(E_sparse_mm)(p))
Running this will output:
E_dense(p): 47.8782
∇E_dense(p): 14.0479
----------------------------------------------------
E_sparse(p): 47.8782
∇E_sparse(p): 14.0479
----------------------------------------------------
E_dense_mm(p): 47.8782
[mm_dense_bwd] partial1:
[[ 26.42007    39.630104 ]
 [ -8.24814   -12.3722105]]
∇E_dense_mm(p): 14.0479
----------------------------------------------------
E_sparse_mm(p): 47.8782
[mm_sparse_bwd] partial1:
[[ 26.42007    39.630104 ]
 [ -8.24814   -12.3722105]]
∇E_sparse_mm(p): -37.6896

We can see that the ∇E_sparse_mm(p): -37.6896 is incorrect, yet the [mm_sparse_bwd] partial1: is computed to be the same as the dense version.
It gets very interesting if you start commenting out the 🥝 and 🍌 lines. The 🥝 line computes the wrongly transposed partial1 yet results in the correct ∇E_sparse_mm:
[mm_sparse_bwd] partial1:
[[ 26.42007    -8.24814  ]
 [ 39.630104  -12.3722105]]
∇E_sparse_mm(p): 14.0479

Adding another transpose .T (🍌 ) doesn't seem to have an effect on the ∇E_sparse_mm but it flips the partial1 back to being correct.
[mm_sparse_bwd] partial1:
[[ 26.42007    39.630104 ]
 [ -8.24814   -12.3722105]]
∇E_sparse_mm(p): 14.0479

I believe this is a bug within Jax (but would be happy to find out I'm doing something wrong/unexpected).

FWIW, I have a guess that this might be due to transposes being tracked with a Bool flag and not being read correctly during the gradient tracing. I have no basis for this but just a hunch based on working with other sparse matrix libraries.

What jax/jaxlib version are you using?
jaxv0.3.14
Which accelerator(s) are you using?
CPU
Additional system info
python 3.8 on mac os 12.6 M1
NVIDIA GPU info
No response

Python 3.11 will be released on October 24 (https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3110rc2).
The ABI is stable, so we are free to build and release wheels using the rc2 release. JAX already works and the tests pass. NumPy and SciPy have already released Python 3.11 wheels.
We should add Python 3.11 wheels to our jaxlib release process.

Description
I see that whenever I use in_place update on an array created inside jit, I get constant-folding that increases compilation time considerably.
This can be seen in the following example:
import jax
import time

@jax.jit
def foo():
    x = jax.numpy.ones((500, 500, 500))
    x = x.at[(100, 100, 100)].set(2)
    return x

for _ in range(2):
    start = time.time()
    _ = foo().block_until_ready()
    print(f'Time elapsed: {time.time()-start:.3}s')
the output looks like:
2022-10-13 11:07:46.573300: E external/org_tensorflow/tensorflow/compiler/xla/service/slow_operation_alarm.cc:65] Constant folding an instruction is taking > 1s:

  dynamic-update-slice.1 (displaying the full instruction incurs a runtime overhead. Raise your logging level to 4 or above).

This isn't necessarily a bug; constant-folding is inherently a trade-off between compilation time and speed at runtime.  XLA has some guards that attempt to keep constant folding from taking too long, but fundamentally you'll always be able to come up with an input program that takes a long time.

If you'd like to file a bug, run with envvar XLA_FLAGS=--xla_dump_to=/tmp/foo and attach the results.

I am creating two seperate samplers with different parameters. The samplers are initialized inside two separate Learner classes. However, if I create individual samplers and provide the two seperate parameters, they both sample from the same distribution.
The weird behavior is present in the following function:
  def __init__(self, key, score_fn, parameters, epsilon, sigmas, data_shape, data_for_bounds=None):
      L = len(sigmas)
      self.L = L
      self.epsilon = epsilon
      self.sigmas = sigmas
      self.score_fn = score_fn

      def langevin_step(params, key, x, step_idx, alpha):
          key, split = jax.random.split(key)
          # draw a normal noise
          noise = jax.random.normal(split, x.shape)
          x_t = x + alpha * self.score_fn(params, x, jnp.repeat(step_idx, x.shape[0])) + jnp.sqrt(2 * alpha) * noise
          return x_t

      def annealed_langevin(params, key, x):
          def langevin_t(key_x_t, l_i):
              key, x_t = key_x_t
              key, split = jax.random.split(key)
              alpha = epsilon * (self.sigmas[l_i] ** 2) / (self.sigmas[0] ** 2)
              x = langevin_step(params, split, x_t, l_i, alpha)
              return (key, x), x
          (_, final_x), path = jax.lax.scan(langevin_t, (key, x), jnp.arange(self.L)[::-1])
          return final_x, path

      self.langevin_fn = jax.jit(annealed_langevin)
      # self.langevin_fn = annealed_langevin
      self.key = key
      self.params = parameters
      self.bounds = None
      if data_for_bounds is not None:
          bounds_min, bounds_max = data_for_bounds.min(axis=0), data_for_bounds.max(axis=0)
          self.bounds = (bounds_min, bounds_max, data_for_bounds.shape[1])
      else:
          print('Bounds not specified')
      # Initialize the variables by calling
      self.langevin_fn(self.params, self.key, jnp.zeros(data_shape))

Hello,
See the screenshot below. Basically, I'm timing some very simple function, whose input is the slice of an array. However, if the input is a jax array, it's much slower than if it's a numpy array, or if I explicitly convert the jax array to a numpy array.


Do you consider this a bug, or is this just some unavoidable overhead of jax arrays?


In this case, would you recommend always converting them to numpy arrays? Here I have no issues computing the jitted f(x) and its Jacobian, but are there any potential side effects when converting the input to numpy arrays?


This might be related to #12198, but here I'm doing repeated slicing of the same indices, not different ones.

Description
The following code in jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
a = jnp.array([5], dtype=jnp.int8)
b = jnp.array([26], dtype=jnp.int8)
print(jnp.lcm(a, b))
produces [126]
while in numpy (checked in 1.23.0 and 1.21.6) (and pytorch 1.11 and 1.12 ) it gives [-126] keeping true to the overflow for an int8 dtype.
Is this difference of results between np and jnp desired here?
Surely, jax.numpy cannot follow NumPy API in every single output but this is something achievable in this case.
The cause is perhaps that jax uses abs at the end of lcm operation. I suppose it should suffice to apply abs on x1 and x2 as gcd does.
Note: Mathematically lcm(5,26)=130, so getting a negative value (as with numpy) can at least signal a warning but getting a positive (but incorrect) value close to the correct value can easily mislead.
int8 dtype was just picked for the sake of simpler example but I am guessing this won't be restricted to int8 dtype.
If you want then I can create a PR for this and in case I m totally mistakened please do enlighten me. Thank you very much.

Description
I was running into an issue that I could condense to an elementary example. It seems to me as if closing over large constants in lax.cond creates a memory leak.
I've reported a similar issue concerning lax.fori_loop in #11448 which was solved in PR #11461. However, my followup post in the original issue got no attention so I decided to close the original issue since the originally reported issue was fixed and to open this one. I hope that is ok.
I'm aware that closing over large constant is not recommended and instead they should be passed as arguments. Nonetheless, this leaking behaviour is unexpected. Maybe it can be -- similar to #11448 --  easily fixed taking weak references to true_fun and false_fun.
MRE
The side-effect-free function leak creates in ints body a large constant and later compiles a function which closes over the large constant within a lax.cond statement. The compiled function called. When leaving the function leak, all references to the large constant are destroyed, including the closure and the compiled closure and the memory should be freed. However, it is not.
import numpy as np
import jax
import psutil


def print_mem_usage() -> None:    
    print(
        f"Resident memory: {psutil.Process().memory_info().rss // (1024 * 1024)} MB"
    )

def print_live_buffers() -> None:
    lbs = jax.lib.xla_bridge.get_backend().live_buffers()
    print(f"Number live buffers: {len(lbs)}")
    for idx, lb in enumerate(lbs):
        print(f"\tlbs[{idx}]: shape {lb.shape} at 0x{lb.unsafe_buffer_pointer():x}")


def print_num_live_executables() -> None:
    les = jax.lib.xla_bridge.get_backend().live_executables()
    print(f"Number live executables: {len(les)}")



def leak():
    # ~ 1 GB of float32s
    size = 1024 * 1024 * 1024 // 4
    data = jax.device_put(np.empty((size, ), dtype=np.float32) + 1)
    
    def g():
        return jax.lax.cond(
            True,
            lambda: data[0],
            lambda: data[1],
        )


    jg = jax.jit(g)

    _ = jg().block_until_ready()

    del g, jg, data, _


def run() -> None:
    for iter in range(5):
        print(f"iter: {iter} ================================================================")
        print_mem_usage()
        _ = leak()
        print_mem_usage()
        print_live_buffers()
        print_num_live_executables()
        

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Description
When using GDA, if you have a case where one of your mesh axes is of size 1, the GDA output by pjit will sometimes ignore the provided pspec and just return a prefix pspec that doesn't include the size=1 mesh axis.
In particular, for an output with shape (128, 128) partitioned according to ('data', 'model'), then if the model axis is size 1, it will return one that it says is partitioned according to ('data',). This is all well and good except if you continue to pass in pspecs to pjit, as below. This behavior makes it harder to develop code that works for cases where the model axis is size 1 vs not size 1 (and where you're evolving your code base from pre-GDA to GDA)
(Should I just be using jax.Array? they seemed even more experimental than GDAs)
(Run with XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=8, or adjust to suit)
import jax
from jax.experimental.global_device_array import GlobalDeviceArray
from jax.random import PRNGKey
import jax.random as jrandom
from jax.experimental.pjit import pjit
from jax.interpreters.pxla import Mesh, PartitionSpec
import numpy as np

jax.config.update("jax_parallel_functions_output_gda", True)

# OK:
# mesh_shape (4, 2)
mesh_shape = (8, 1)

devices = jax.devices()

mesh = Mesh(np.array(devices).reshape(mesh_shape), ('data', 'model'))

key = PRNGKey(0)

with mesh:
    def f():
        return jrandom.normal(key, (128, 128))
    # GDA tupleizes the args here, which is fine
    desired_pspec = PartitionSpec( ('data', ),('model', ))

    f_pjit = pjit(f, in_axis_resources=None, out_axis_resources=desired_pspec)

    out: GlobalDeviceArray = f_pjit()
    assert out.shape == (128, 128)
    # BOOM
    assert out.mesh_axes == desired_pspec, f"{out.mesh_axes} != {desired_pspec}"

    def g(a):
        return a + a

    g_pjit = pjit(g, in_axis_resources=desired_pspec, out_axis_resources=desired_pspec)

    # also BOOM!
    out2: GlobalDeviceArray = g_pjit(out)
    # ValueError: Got an input GDA to pjit with different partitioning than specified in the in_axis_resources argument to pjit. The partitioning must match, or use `jax.experimental.pjit.FROM_GDA` in `in_axis_resources` for GDA. Got GDA sharding: MeshPspecSharding(mesh={'data': 8, 'model': 1}, partition_spec=PartitionSpec(('data',),)) and pjit sharding: MeshPspecSharding(mesh={'data': 8, 'model': 1}, partition_spec=PartitionSpec(('data',), ('model',)))

Hi,
we are facing strange behavior when using collective ops. Whenever a pmapped function includes jax.lax.all_gather or jax.lax.ppermute, the compilation of said function will stall indefinitely at 100% GPU utilization. However, the collective ops jax.lax.psum, jax.lax.pmean, jax.lax.pmin, jax.lax.pmax work fine.
Setup of the server/versions of the software:


Ubuntu 20.04



Nvidia Driver Version 515.65.01



CUDA Version: 11.7



8x NVIDIA A6000



jax 0.3.21, jaxlib 0.3.20



We tried installing jax/jaxlib both using the pip installation and building it from source. In the latter case, we manually install NCCL 2.13.4 before building jax/jaxlib from source. Both approaches yield the same outcome. We got the idea to build jax/jaxlib from source after reading the threads about similar issues #10969, #11637. Also, using different CUDA versions did not help.
E.g., this simple code snippet will produce a deadlock.
import os
import jax
import numpy as np
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "0,1"
x = np.arange(2)
y = jax.pmap(lambda x: jax.lax.all_gather(x, axis_name='i'), axis_name='i')(x)
However, this code snippet works just fine:
x = np.arange(2)
y = jax.pmap(lambda x: jax.lax.pmin(x, axis_name='i'), axis_name='i')(x)

Description
Hey, I'm a big fan of JAX and have run into an issue recently: when I run simple JAX commands inside a Docker container (whose host machine is a GCP TPU VM with type v2-8), I get a strange segmentation error.
Minimum reproducible example
I did the following steps:

Create a TPU VM (on GCP)

gcloud alpha compute tpus tpu-vm create NAME-OF-TPU --zone us-central1-f \
        --accelerator-type v2-8 \
        --version v2-alpha


Connect to the TPU VM via SSH
Pull a simple Python image and run the container:

sudo docker run --privileged -it --rm python:3.8 bash


Install the latest version of JAX:

pip install jax[tpu]==0.3.19 -f https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/libtpu_releases.html


Open Python inside the container and run some commands:

import jax
jax.local_devices()  # This works.

While I was learning jax, I found a strange behaviour when testing the single-process multiple-data (SPMD) programs on my local Tesla K80 (I believe this is a single board with two GPU chips). The docstring for jax.numpy.linalg.cholesky seems to be copied from its NumPy counterpart, where it states:

... No checking is performed to verify whether a is Hermitian or not. ...

However, the actual implementation in jax/_src/lax/linalg.py does indeed always symmetrize the input matrix. Its argument symmetrize_input, which controls whether symmetrization happens, defaults to True and is not exposed to the end user.
IMHO this has two consequences:

Users can be misled and confused by the behavior of the method.
Symmetrization may introduce unnecessary overhead when the input matrix is already Hermitian.

Description
vmap seems to convert its arguments to traced arrays. I would argue that this is unexpected behavior. Let me give an example:
Let us assume that I want to calculate the slope of triangles:
def f(ax,bx, ay,by):
    
    dx = bx - ax
    dy = by - ay
    
    return(dy / dx)
The x-size of the triangles is known at compile time. Jax correctly identifies this and replaces dx with a constant:
> print(jax.make_jaxpr(partial(f,0.0,1.0))(0.0,1.0)))
{ lambda ; a:f32[] b:f32[]. let c:f32[] = sub b a; d:f32[] = div c 1.0 in (d,) }
Now let us assume that we want to do this multiple times on triangles of different sizes.
> print(jax.make_jaxpr(partial(vmap(f), np.array([0.0,1.0]), np.array([1.0,3.0])))(np.array([0.0,0.0]), np.array([1.0,1.0])))
{ lambda a:f32[2] b:f32[2]; c:f32[2] d:f32[2]. let
    e:f32[2] = sub a b
    f:f32[2] = sub d c
    g:f32[2] = div f e
  in (g,) }
JAX fails to fold bx - ax into a constant. To be fair, I have no idea how a constant array would work in the IR, but I would argue that this is unexpected behavior, is it?
What jax/jaxlib version are you using?
jax v0.3.17, jaxlib v0.3.15

CPU

Python 3.10.7, Archlinux (latest as of 2022-09-25)

nodes.bodyText:
Consider the following code fragment:
x = load_checkpoint()

@partial(pjit, in_axis_resources=in_sharding, out_axis_resources=out_sharding):
def foo(a)
  return a + x

y = load_another_checkpoint()
z = foo(y)
The call to foo(y) fails if the value of x is sharded over multiple hosts.
One scenario when supporting this would be very useful is if one need to close over a large static model in order to adapt to the interface required by an existing library they use. E.g. assume one wants to use the XTraner class below, which is a part of a library they don't have control over. I.e. they can't modify or extend XTrainer or loss_fn.
@dataclass
class XTrainer:
  loss_fn: Callable[[Prediction, BatchType], LossValue]
  
  @partial(pjit, ...)
  def train_step(self, input_batch: BatchType, train_state: TrainState) -> TrainState:
    """Performs a single gradient descent step on the model represented with `train_state`.
       Runs a prediction in the model and computes the value of the loss by calling `loss_fn`.
    """
    ...
There are cases in which one would want to exercise a static pre-trained model inside the implementation of loss_fn. Some that come to mind are:

One wants to train from human feedback as in InstructGPT.
One wants to distill the trained model to be close to a target, pre-trained model.

Unfortunately, if the static model needs to be sharded over multiple hosts, this is currently not supported and AFAIK, one can't use XTrainer without modification in this case.
nodes.title: Allow pjit to close over values sharded on multiple devices

Description
The code below computes an element on the diagonal of a pairwise distance matrix, with a modified sqrt function that has finite gradients at 0. Without JIT, the gradients wrt inputs are 0., as expected. With JIT, the gradients are ~1e12.
This shows up in TFP-on-JAX's GaussianProcess. As a workaround, we can set the diagonal of the distance matrix to 0 (which zeros out the gradients), but that doesn't account for the case where the input array has duplicate points (so zeros can appear elsewhere in the distance matrix). This is blocking Vizier's use of TFP-on-JAX's GP.
import jax
from jax import numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

x = jnp.array(
    [-1.152883 , -1.229587 , -0.7161828,  1.6050261, -0.9966271, 1.0175147])

@jax.custom_gradient
def sqrt_with_finite_grads(x):
  """Avoid NaN gradients when `x == 0`."""
  def grad(grad_ys):
    large_float_like_x = np.sqrt(np.finfo(x.dtype).max)

    # In this repro, x == 0, so safe_grads = large_float_like_x.
    safe_grads = jnp.where(
        jnp.equal(x, 0.), large_float_like_x, 0.5 / jnp.sqrt(x))
    return grad_ys * safe_grads
  return jnp.sqrt(x), grad

def dist(x):
  """Stripped down from https://github.com/tensorflow/probability/blob/main/tensorflow_probability/python/math/psd_kernels/internal/util.py#L191"""
  # These two terms are equal. If we compute them differently (`sum(x*x)`, `dot(x, x)`, `sum(x**2)`) the issue persists. If we compute them the same way, the issue disappears.
  # (This is how we compute the diagonal of a squared distance matrix, when both inputs are the same.)
  row_norm_x = 2. * jnp.sum(x**2, axis=-1)
  middle_term = 2. * jnp.dot(x, x)

  # Their difference is 0.
  out = row_norm_x - middle_term
  d = jnp.clip(out, 0., jnp.inf)

  # Clipping at a very small value, instead of 0., appears to fix it. (Because `clip` zeros out the gradient when the value is outside the interval?)
  # d = jnp.clip(out, 1e-30, jnp.inf)

  return sqrt_with_finite_grads(d)

print('No jit grads: ', jax.grad(dist)(x))  # => [0., 0., ...]
print('Jit grads: ', jax.jit(jax.grad(dist))(x))  # => [-1.9e12, -1.7e12, ...]

nodes.bodyText:
This issue is the result of some pair-debugging with @sharadmv.
In the course of trying to re-land #12091, I found that it was leading to some test timeouts due to replacing lax.gather with lax.slice. This issue actually can be reproduced in the current release of JAX; given the current implementation, we can define two functions, one of which takes the gather path and one of which takes the slice path:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax

def index_via_gather(x):
  return x[(0,)]

def index_via_slice(x):
  return x[0]

x = jnp.arange(100)

print(jax.make_jaxpr(index_via_gather)(x))
# { lambda ; a:i32[100]. let
#     b:i32[1] = broadcast_in_dim[broadcast_dimensions=() shape=(1,)] 0
#     c:i32[] = gather[
#       dimension_numbers=GatherDimensionNumbers(offset_dims=(), collapsed_slice_dims=(0,), start_index_map=(0,))
#       fill_value=None
#       indices_are_sorted=True
#       mode=GatherScatterMode.PROMISE_IN_BOUNDS
#       slice_sizes=(1,)
#       unique_indices=True
#     ] a b
#   in (c,) }

print(jax.make_jaxpr(index_via_slice)(x))
# { lambda ; a:i32[100]. let
#     b:i32[1] = slice[limit_indices=(1,) start_indices=(0,) strides=(1,)] a
#     c:i32[] = squeeze[dimensions=(0,)] b
#   in (c,) }
The latter slice behavior was added in #11867 because it can be more efficient.
Unfortunately, there is a catch: when indexing is done repeatedly on different static indices, the slice approach has a cache miss on each new index, making it much slower. The test that led to the rollback of #12091 exposed this issue, which we can reproduce for the current implementation like this:
def f_gather(x):
  return jnp.array([x[(i,)] for i in range(len(x))])

def f_slice(x):
  return jnp.array([x[i] for i in range(len(x))])

x = jnp.arange(500)

%timeit -n 1 -r 1 f_gather(x).block_until_ready()
# 611 ms ± 0 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 1 run, 1 loop each)

%timeit -n 1 -r 1 f_slice(x).block_until_ready()
# 6.78 s ± 0 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 1 run, 1 loop each)
Repeated indexing via static slice is very slow comparted to repeated indexing via gather.
We could instead consider using lax.dynamic_slice, which has comparable performance to gather for this repeated operation:
def f_dynamic_slice(x):
  return jnp.array([jax.lax.dynamic_index_in_dim(x, i, 0) for i in range(len(x))])

%timeit -n 1 -r 1 f_dynamic_slice(x).block_until_ready()
# 420 ms ± 0 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 1 run, 1 loop each)
Any thoughts? cc/ @mattjj, who contributed #11867
nodes.title: slice-based indexing is slow for repeated indexing
